notes:
Here is a verse-by-verse commentary on Luke 15, drawn from the sources I was able to search and read, with URLs for each point.

---

## Luke 15:1–3 — The Occasion

**v. 1:** "Now all the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to listen to Jesus."

- The Greek verb "were coming near" (eggizō) is in the present tense, indicating they were continually drawing near to Jesus throughout His ministry. Tax collectors (telōnai) were Jews who collected taxes for Rome and were despised as traitors who often enriched themselves by overcharging. "Sinners" here refers to those who did not observe the Pharisaic rules of purity — the *am ha'aretz*, "people of the land" (Precept Austin, citing Gary Inrig). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-15-commentary]
- These outcasts "had ears to hear," directly responding to Jesus' closing call in Luke 14:35: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Leon Morris, cited at Precept Austin). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-15-commentary]
- Ellicott notes that the publicans and sinners knew Jesus had turned in indignation from the Pharisee's house (Luke 14), and this gave them courage to approach Him. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 2:** "So the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble: 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.'"

- The word "man" is not in the Greek — they said "this" (houtos), a term of contempt meaning "this fellow." They took Jesus to be a mere man (Gill). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/15.htm]
- Table fellowship in that culture signified acceptance and approval. The Pharisees' complaint was that Jesus not only tolerated sinners but enjoyed their company (Precept Austin, citing Gary Inrig). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-15-commentary]
- Ellicott suggests these were likely some of the same guests from the Pharisee's dinner in Luke 14, who had followed Jesus to observe Him. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 3:** "Then Jesus told them this parable."

- The singular "parable" (parabolēn) covers all three stories that follow — the lost sheep, lost coin, and lost (prodigal) son. They form "an artistically constructed unit with a single theme" — God's joy when He finds a lost sinner (I.H. Marshall, cited at Precept Austin). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-15-commentary]
- The parables were spoken to the Pharisees for their conviction, and to the publicans and sinners for their encouragement (Gill). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/15.htm]

---

## Luke 15:4–7 — The Lost Sheep

**v. 4:** "What man among you, if he has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?"

- Jesus uses a rhetorical question that draws the hearers in. The shepherd leaving ninety-nine seems reckless, but the point is not about neglect of the majority — the safety of the ninety-nine is assumed, and the focus is on the joy of recovery (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- "No creature strays more easily than a sheep; none is more heedless; and none so incapable of finding its way back to the flock" (Adam Clarke, cited at Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- Gill argues the "ninety-nine" are not angels (angels are never called sheep, and fallen angels are not sought and saved), nor are they elect believers. Rather, they represent the self-righteous Scribes and Pharisees who were "left in the wilderness" — a state of unregeneracy where nothing is sown or planted, no seed of grace exists. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/15.htm]
- By contrast, Ellicott sees a "legitimate extension" of the parable: the ninety-nine as the hosts of unfallen angels, and the one lost sheep as collective humanity. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- Jesus taught something revolutionary: God actively seeks out the lost. Many rabbis believed God received the sinner who came the right way, but "God finds the sinner more than the sinner does find God" (Enduring Word, citing William Barclay). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 5:** "And when he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders."

- The shepherd does not drive the sheep before him or make it walk on its own — he carries it. This shows the passiveness of the sinner in conversion, human weakness, and the strength and love of Christ (Gill). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/15.htm]
- Ellicott draws a three-fold application: (a) Jesus' love for each wandering soul, bearing and sustaining it in weakness; (b) His taking on our nature and bearing its infirmities; (c) those with the mind of Christ following in His footsteps. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 6:** "comes home, and calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!'"

- The "home" in the spiritual sense is either the church (Zion) or heaven itself, whither Christ brings His found sheep (Gill). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/15.htm]
- Ellicott notes the recurrence of "friends and neighbours" from Luke 14:12. The "friends and neighbours" of Christ may be the disciples He chose, and also the angels and spirits of the just made perfect. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 7:** "In the same way, I tell you that there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent."

- The "ninety-nine just persons who need no repentance" is not a statement that some people are without sin. It is a "grave and indignant protest, veiled under the form of an apparent concession, against the self-righteousness of the Pharisees" (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- Jesus mentions repentance here even though the sheep in the parable does nothing to repent. It is "almost as if He said, 'the sheep doesn't repent, but you need to when God finds you'" (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- According to Barclay, many religious people of Jesus' day had a saying: "There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who is obliterated before God." Jesus reversed this entirely — joy in heaven is over the sinner who repents, not who is destroyed. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

---

## Luke 15:8–10 — The Lost Coin

**v. 8:** "Or what woman who has ten silver coins and loses one of them does not light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it?"

- The coin is a drachma, worth about a day's wage. Some suggest it may have been part of a silver chain worn as a head-ornament marking a married woman, making the loss more severe (Enduring Word, citing Bruce). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- Ellicott notes several symbolic details: the coin bears the king's image, just as the human soul bears the image of the great King. The coin is lost *in the house* (unlike the sheep that strayed from the fold), suggesting a soul can be lost even within the visible church. The woman (rather than a man) represents the need for "feminine" virtues in soul-winning: patience, diligence, minute observation. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- "Light a lamp" = put forth the full power of truth and holiness; "sweep the house" = use all available means. In church life, this is faithful preaching (the lamp) and faithful organization of charity (the sweeping) (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- The coin, though lost, still belongs to the woman. Spurgeon observed: "The piece of silver was lost but still claimed. Observe that the woman called the money, 'my piece which was lost.' When she lost its possession she did not lose her right to it" (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 9:** "And when she finds it, she calls together her friends and neighbors to say, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost coin.'"

- The joy is natural and overflowing. In the same way, God is happy when sinners repent, in sharp contrast to the religious leaders who complained (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 10:** "In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God's angels over one sinner who repents."

- The phrase "in the presence of God's angels" suggests the joy is God's own joy, shared before His angels, not merely joy *among* the angels (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- We seldom think of God as rejoicing, but Scripture elsewhere confirms it: "As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you" (Isaiah 62:5); "He will rejoice over you with singing" (Zephaniah 3:17) (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

---

## Luke 15:11–16 — The Prodigal Son: Departure and Ruin

**v. 11:** "Then Jesus said, 'There was a man who had two sons.'"

- In the immediate application, the father is God, the elder son represents the respectably religious Pharisees, and the younger stands for the publicans and sinners. On a wider scale, the elder son may stand for Israel according to the flesh, and the younger for the Gentile world (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- Ellicott notes it is "obvious" from the parable's structure that the elder son cannot represent unfallen angels, which "tells against that interpretation of the ninety and nine sheep or the nine pieces of silver." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary identifies "that certain man" as God the Father, the self-righteous older son as the Jews, and the younger as the Gentiles who came to receive Him (Acts 15:14). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/luke-15.html]

**v. 12:** "The younger son said to him, 'Father, give me my share of the estate.' So he divided his property between them."

- Under normal Jewish custom, a father could grant inheritance before or after death, but after death was typical. The younger son's request was for a special exception, motivated by foolishness and greed (Enduring Word, citing Geldenhuys). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- In the normal distribution, the elder son would receive two-thirds, the younger one-third (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- The father "divided to them his livelihood" — he divided his property between *both* sons, meaning the elder son now also had his portion, though he remained at home (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- The father's love "allowed rebellion and, in some sense, respected human will." He knew the request was foolish but let the son go (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 13:** "After a few days, the younger son got everything together and journeyed to a distant country, where he squandered his wealth in wild living."

- The younger son represents the temper that is eager for independence, self-asserting, energetic — contrasted with the elder son's contemplative, devout, quiescent character (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- The Greek word translated "wild" or "riotous" living is *asōtōs*, meaning prodigal, thriftless, wasteful (Ellicott). The English word "prodigal" means recklessly extravagant. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- The "far country" spiritually represents estrangement from God — a state in which the human spirit wanders far off from the Father (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 14:** "After he had spent all he had, a severe famine swept through that country, and he began to be in need."

- The son was entirely to blame for the wasteful spending, but not for the famine. Both his own sin and circumstances beyond his control contributed to his misery (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- Spiritually, the "mighty famine" is the yearning of the soul's unsatisfied desire — "not a famine of bread…but of hearing the words of the LORD" (Amos 8:11) (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 15:** "So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed the pigs."

- The verb "joined himself" (literally "clave to") is the same word used of a husband cleaving to his wife (Matthew 19:5), expressing the absolute dependence of the famished man (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- Feeding swine would have been horrifying to Jesus' Jewish audience, since pigs were unclean under the Law (Leviticus 11:7). This represents the lowest possible degradation for a son of Abraham (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- Spiritually, this pictures a state in which a person's will and energies have only one work: ministering to baser appetites (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 16:** "He longed to fill his belly with the pods the pigs were eating, but no one would give him a thing."

- The "pods" (*keratia*) are the long bean-like pods of the carob tree (also called St. John's bread), commonly used as swine food in Syria and Egypt. They contain saccharine matter but are not sufficient human food (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- Spiritually, these husks represent sensual pleasures in which those who are "as the swine, identified with brute appetites, find adequate sustenance." But the soul born for a higher inheritance cannot satisfy itself with them (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- The phrase "no one gave him anything" underscores the complete abandonment the son now experienced. His "friends" from the wild living were gone; the citizen gave only the job, not kindness (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

---

## Luke 15:17–19 — The Prodigal's Repentance

**v. 17:** "Finally he came to his senses and said, 'How many of my father's hired servants have plenty of food? But here I am, starving to death!'"

- "He came to himself" (Greek: *eis heauton elthōn*) means he woke as from an evil dream and became conscious of his true self. In his rebellion and disobedience, "he wasn't himself." The real man was the penitent, not the prodigal (Enduring Word, citing Morrison). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- He did not blame his father, his brother, his friends, his boss, or the pigs. He recognized his misery without dwelling on it, and focused on his father (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- The "hired servants" (*misthioi*) were day-labourers, lower than household slaves who were in some sense part of the family. The hired servant could be dismissed at a day's notice (Enduring Word, citing Barclay). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 18:** "I will get up and go back to my father and say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.'"

- The son's focus was on returning to his *father*, not merely to his village or home. We must come back to God first and foremost, before coming back to church or Christian friends (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- "I have sinned against heaven" — the Greek literally says "I sinned" (aorist), going back in thought to the first act of sin as containing all that grew from it. "Against heaven" is a reverent circumlocution for "against God" (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- MacArthur notes that the prodigal trusted his father's mercy and goodness, evidenced in how the father treated even the lowest people. He said in effect, "I'm going to trust my father's nature." [https://www.gty.org/sermons/GTY104/the-tale-of-two-sons]

**v. 19:** "I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants."

- The son asked for two things across his story: first, "Father, give me" (v.12); now, "Father, make me." Only the second request brought joy (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- The son would not even ask to be treated as a son but as a hired servant. This is complete humility and an honest confession of unworthiness (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

---

## Luke 15:20–24 — The Father's Welcome

**v. 20:** "So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him."

- The prodigal did not merely think about repenting — he acted. Spurgeon warned: "Some of you whom I now address have been thinking, and thinking, and thinking, till I fear that you will think yourselves into perdition" (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- That the father *ran* was extraordinary — grown men in that culture did not run; it was considered undignified. This pictures God's eagerness to welcome the repentant sinner (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- The Greek tense indicates the father "repeatedly kissed" him (*katephilēsen*) (Enduring Word, citing Morris). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- The father saw the son "while he was still a great way off" — the father had been watching, waiting, never forgetting. The love was proactive, not merely receptive (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- Ellicott adds: the penitent is "poor in spirit…conscious of his nakedness" and yet "a great way off" — not yet near the home of peace — but "even there, there comes to him the joy of all joys, the love of the Father finds him." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 21:** "The son declared, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.'"

- The son began his prepared speech but notably *omitted* the final line — "Make me like one of your hired servants." Ellicott observes: "Now that he has seen his father, he cannot bring himself to say again, 'Make me as one of thy hired servants.'" Having felt the Father's kiss, though still confessing unworthiness, "they cannot be satisfied with anything less than sonship." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 22:** "But the father said to his servants, 'Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet.'"

- None of these four items were necessities — they were all gifts to honour the son and demonstrate love (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- Ellicott gives specific symbolic meanings: the "best robe" = the garment of praise, the vesture of righteousness (Isaiah 61:3); the "ring" = the signet ring of special favour, the seal of "calling and election" (Jeremiah 22:24); the "sandals" = the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace (Ephesians 6:15). Slaves went barefoot; sandals signified sonship. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 23:** "Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate."

- The definite article "the" fatted calf suggests one kept ready for a special feast of joy. It answers to the "feast of fat things" of Isaiah 25:6 — the joy of full fruition of God's presence (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- Ellicott notes that the word for "kill" (*thysate*) is the technical term for slaying a sacrificial victim, hinting that such a feast was only possible through sacrifice and death. The fatted calf thus prefigures the Eucharistic feast. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]

**v. 24:** "For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!' So they began to celebrate."

- "Dead" expresses the father's perception during the son's absence — alienation and self-chosen shame had made the father think of him as dead. Death would have been easier to bear (Ellicott). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
- MacArthur summarizes that this young man "receives reconciliation, restoration, forgiveness, sonship, and all he does is trust his father and repent of his sin. He has no plan for restitution, no works. This is grace." [https://www.gty.org/sermons/GTY104/the-tale-of-two-sons]

## Luke 15:25–32 — The Older Brother

**v. 25–26:** "Meanwhile the older son was in the field, and as he approached the house, he heard music and dancing. So he called one of the servants and asked what was going on."

- The older son was hard at work in the field, having never lived a prodigal life. He heard "music and dancing" (*symphōnias kai chorōn*) — a full celebration with instrumental music and dancing, typical of a wedding feast (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 27:** "'Your brother has returned,' he said, 'and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has him back safe and sound.'"

- The servant's words are straightforward and joyful, emphasizing the reason for celebration: the brother is back "safe and sound" (Greek: *hygiainonta*, "in good health"). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 28:** "The older son became angry and refused to go in. So his father came out and pleaded with him."

- This is the pivotal moment: the older brother mirrors exactly the Pharisees standing aloof in v.2, grumbling while Jesus eats with sinners. John Piper notes: "In Luke 15:1–2, the Pharisees are standing aloof, grumbling about the meal Jesus is sharing with the sinners. And in Luke 15:28, the older brother is standing aloof, angry and unwilling to join the father who is eating with the younger brother." [https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-tender-word-for-pharisees]
- The father "came out and pleaded with him" — the same father who ran to the younger son now goes out to the older son. Both sons are loved and sought (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- MacArthur says "the main reason Jesus told the parable" was to address the elder brother's attitude — the central lesson is the contrast between God's delight in redemption and the Pharisees' inflexible hostility. [https://www.gty.org/articles/A115/an-unforgettable-tale]

**v. 29:** "But he answered his father, 'Look, all these years I have served you and never disobeyed a commandment of yours. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends.'"

- The older son uses the language of a slave, not a son: "I have *served* you" (Greek: *douleuō*, to serve as a slave) and "never disobeyed a *commandment*" (*entolēn*). John Piper observes: "The problem is that the older brother related to his father as slave to a master, not as son to a father. His father was merely a command-giver, and he was a command-keeper. And therefore, merit, not mercy, was the foundation of the relationship; and mercy to the undeserving made him angry." [https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-tender-word-for-pharisees]
- His exaggerations are typical of bitterness: "I *never* transgressed…you *never* gave." The older son had done damage in his heart over many years (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- "The proud and the self-righteous always feel that they are not treated as well as they deserve" (Enduring Word, citing Morris). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 30:** "But when this son of yours returns from squandering your wealth with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

- The older brother refuses to say "my brother" — he says "this son of yours." He distances himself from both his father and his brother (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- He accuses the younger son of consorting with prostitutes, a detail not mentioned in the earlier narrative. Whether he knew this for a fact or assumed the worst, it reveals the older brother's judgmental heart (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 31:** "'Son, you are always with me,' the father said, 'and all that is mine is yours.'"

- The Greek word is *teknon* ("child"), not *huios* ("son") — "child is a word of tenderest affection" (Enduring Word, citing Morrison). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- "All that is mine is yours" — the older son had full access to everything the father owned. His complaint about never getting a young goat was not due to the father's stinginess but his own failure to ask or receive. This is the tragedy of the self-righteous: they live in the father's house but fail to understand the father's heart (Enduring Word, citing Morgan). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

**v. 32:** "But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.'"

- The father gently but firmly corrects: not "this son of yours" but "this *brother of yours*." The older son must learn to see the prodigal as family, not as an outsider (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- The parable ends without resolution — we never learn whether the older son went in. Jesus leaves the question hanging before the Pharisees: will you enter the celebration, or remain outside grumbling? (Enduring Word, implied). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown summarize the lessons: "(1) The deeper sunk and the longer estranged any sinner is, the more exuberant is the joy which his recovery occasions. (2) Such joy is not the portion of those whose whole lives have been spent in the service of their Father in heaven. (3) Instead of grudging the want of this, they should rejoice." [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Luk/Luk_015.cfm]
- Spurgeon concluded: "The truth here taught is just this: that mercy stretches forth her hand to misery, that grace receives men as sinners, that it deals with demerit, unworthiness and worthlessness; that those who think themselves righteous are not the objects of divine compassion, but the unrighteous, the guilty and the undeserving." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

## Tradition-Specific Readings

### Baptist View (MacArthur / GTY)

John MacArthur emphasizes that the parable is principally a wake-up call about the elder brother, not merely a warm story about the prodigal. The "central and culminating lesson" is the stark contrast between God's delight in redemption and the Pharisees' hostility toward sinners. The elder brother's "cold indifference" was "the real focal point of the story." MacArthur also stresses that the prodigal's restoration was pure grace: "He has no plan for restitution, no works." [https://www.gty.org/articles/A115/an-unforgettable-tale] and [https://www.gty.org/sermons/GTY104/the-tale-of-two-sons]

### Reformed / Sovereign Grace (Piper / Desiring God)

John Piper sees all three parables as revealing Jesus' identity: "I welcome sinners because I am the incarnation of God's love pursuing the lost. I am the shepherd seeking the sheep. I am the woman seeking her coin." Piper emphasizes that Jesus is not passive — "He is looking for them and eagerly awaiting their coming." Regarding the older brother, Piper identifies the core problem as relating to the father "as slave to a master, not as son to a father" — merit rather than mercy. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/coming-to-yourself-and-coming-to-the-father] and [https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-tender-word-for-pharisees]

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

David Guzik (Calvary Chapel tradition) emphasizes the revolutionary nature of Jesus' teaching — that God actively seeks the lost, a truth the rabbis had never emphasized before. The commentary highlights the experiential dimension: the prodigal "came to himself" meaning he thought clearly for the first time; the father's compassion led him to run (undignified for an Eastern man); and the older brother's bitterness reveals how the self-righteous "can live in the father's house yet fail to understand the father's heart." The practical application includes the church's role in seeking the lost, mirroring the Holy Spirit's work. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-15/]

### Older Commentaries: Gill (Particular Baptist, 18th c.)

Gill provides an extensive Calvinistic reading. He identifies the "ninety-nine" not as angels or elect believers but as the self-righteous Pharisees — nominal professors left in the "wilderness" of unregeneracy. The "one lost sheep" is the elect among the Jews, especially the publicans and sinners. Christ goes after them "not because of their number, nor their nature…nor any previous dispositions…but because of His love to them, and the relation between them as shepherd and sheep; and because of His Father's will, and His own obligation by covenant." The coin and sheep do nothing to contribute to being found — conversion is entirely God's work. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/luke/15.htm]

### Older Commentaries: Ellicott (Anglican, 19th c.)

Charles Ellicott offers a more expansive reading. He permits the extension of the ninety-nine to unfallen angels "or unfallen beings more like ourselves in other worlds" — a cosmic redemptive scope. His symbolic reading of details is rich: the "best robe" = righteousness, the "ring" = election, the "sandals" = gospel readiness, the "fatted calf" prefigures the Eucharist. He notes the prodigal dropping "make me a hired servant" after feeling the father's kiss — a psychological insight into genuine repentance. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/15.htm]
